mcqs.question: A production service has a growing static map that's never trimmed. Why doesn't the garbage collector reclaim its old entries?
options: Static fields are excluded from the root set on most runtimes
The collector only runs when free memory drops below a hard threshold
The map's entries have finalizers that block collection indefinitely
Every entry is reachable from the static field, which is a root — the collector correctly treats reachable data as live, regardless of whether it's still useful
mcqs.explanation: A static field is part of the root set, so anything the map holds is legitimately reachable and correctly marked live — this is a logical leak, not a collector malfunction. Static fields are not excluded from roots, collection frequency isn't gated purely on a hard memory threshold, and finalizers aren't the mechanism at play here.

mcqs.question: A `Widget` subscribes to an `EventBus` in its constructor but is never unsubscribed before being dropped by its caller. Why does the Widget keep leaking?
options: The event bus holds a reference to the Widget's callback, keeping the Widget reachable indefinitely even though the caller is done with it
Java automatically retains any object that has ever registered a callback for the process lifetime
The Widget's constructor allocates memory that the destructor never frees
EventBus subscriptions are stored using weak references by default, but this one happens to be strong
mcqs.explanation: The bus's internal subscriber list is exactly the retaining root here — as long as that list holds the callback, the Widget behind it stays reachable no matter what the original caller does. This isn't a language-wide retention rule, and there's no destructor/constructor allocation mismatch involved — the bus's own reference is the entire cause.

mcqs.question: In a heap dump, an object has a tiny shallow size but a retained size of several gigabytes. What does that combination most likely indicate?
options: The retained size figure is a measurement error and should be ignored
The object itself is small, but it dominates a large subtree of other objects that would be freed if it were freed
The object contains a corrupted reference to itself
The object is about to be collected on the next GC pass regardless of its size
mcqs.explanation: Retained size is shallow size plus everything the object dominates in the reference graph, so a small object with huge retained size is almost always a container or cache whose entries would all become unreachable if it were freed — exactly the profile of a leak root. It isn't a measurement artifact, doesn't imply self-reference corruption, and retained size says nothing about imminent collection.

mcqs.question: A service's memory grows steadily and OOMs after a few days. What's the correct first diagnostic step, before touching any GC configuration?
options: Increase the heap size to buy more runway while investigating
Restart the service on a schedule to reset memory usage
Switch to a different collector and observe whether the growth pattern changes
Take two heap dumps under similar load, separated by hours or days, and diff retained size by class to find what's actually growing
mcqs.explanation: Diagnosing which class is genuinely growing and following its dominator tree to a root is the step that actually locates the leak; every other option either masks the symptom (bigger heap, scheduled restarts) or changes an unrelated variable (collector swap) without answering what's retaining the memory.

mcqs.question: A team responds to a memory incident by immediately doubling the heap size and switching collectors, without taking a heap dump first. What's the risk?
options: If there's an actual logical leak underneath, this only delays the same OOM to a later, potentially worse time, without fixing anything
Doubling the heap size always slows down every GC pause regardless of what's actually leaking
Switching collectors can corrupt existing heap data mid-transition
This approach is strictly correct and there's no real risk to flag
mcqs.explanation: Neither a bigger heap nor a different collector addresses a growing set of retained objects — they just change when and how the same underlying leak eventually causes trouble, often with a bigger blast radius later. A bigger heap doesn't inherently slow every pause (that depends on live-set size, not heap size alone), and a collector switch doesn't corrupt data; the real risk is masking, not technical breakage.
